rules.name: Beyond 3σ
rules.text: One measurement far outside the limits. Something was different for that one: find it while people still remember.

rules.name: Shift
rules.signal: {n} points in a row on the same side of the mean (points {from}–{to}).
rules.text: The level has moved. After a change you made, that is proof it worked; without one, find what changed.

rules.name: Trend
rules.signal: {n} points in a row, each {direction} than the one before (points {from}–{to}).
rules.text: Something is drifting: wear, a growing backlog, fatigue, or a slow change in the mix.

rules.name: Sawtooth
rules.signal: {n} points in a row alternating up and down (points {from}–{to}).
rules.text: Up, down, up, down: usually two streams measured in turn (two shifts, two docks, two operators), or over-adjustment after every value.

rules.name: 2 of 3 beyond 2σ
rules.signal: 2 of 3 points beyond 2σ on the same side (points {from}–{to}).
rules.text: A small shift that has not yet crossed the limit. Treat it as an early warning and look at those points.

rules.name: 4 of 5 beyond 1σ
rules.signal: 4 of 5 points beyond 1σ on the same side (points {from}–{to}).
rules.text: The process leans to one side. Often a change in the input, the staffing or the time of day.

rules.name: Too quiet
rules.signal: {n} points in a row within 1σ of the mean (points {from}–{to}).
rules.text: Less variation than this process shows: the measurement may not see the differences, or two streams average each other out.

rules.name: Mixture
rules.signal: {n} points in a row beyond 1σ on both sides, none near the mean (points {from}–{to}).
rules.text: Values jump between two levels: two processes are mixed in one chart. Separate them (by shift, dock, product) and chart each.

control.stable: No signal in {n} measurements. The ups and downs are the normal noise of this process; reacting to single values will not help. To get a better number, change the process itself.
control.signals: {count} signal(s) that are not normal noise. Investigate those measurements first: what was different in volume, people, equipment or method? Then take the cause through 5 Whys.
control.short: Fewer than 20 measurements: the limits are rough. Keep measuring before you trust a signal or a capability index.

capability.none: Enter a specification limit (LSL or USL) to see how capable the process is.

low.label: Not capable
low.text: Cpk {cpk}: the process cannot stay inside the specification. Expect about {ppm} per million outside ({pct}). Reduce the spread or move the mean before anyone promises the customer.

marginal.label: Marginal
marginal.text: Cpk {cpk}: it fits, but only just. Expect about {ppm} per million outside ({pct}); a small drift puts you over the limit. Keep the chart running.

capable.label: Capable
capable.text: Cpk {cpk}: the process fits the specification with room to spare. Expect about {ppm} per million outside ({pct}). Hold the standard and check the chart weekly.

six.label: Six sigma
six.text: Cpk {cpk}: the specification is twice as wide as the process needs. Expect about {ppm} per million outside. Spend the effort elsewhere.

capability.gap: Cp {cp} but Cpk {cpk}: the spread would fit, the process is off centre. Moving the mean towards {target} gains more than reducing variation.
capability.shortLong: Pp/Ppk ({pp}/{ppk}) are well below Cp/Cpk: the process shifts between measurements. The signals on the chart say where.

normality.normal: The values follow a normal curve (Anderson–Darling, {p}): the capability indices and the expected % outside can be trusted.
normality.notNormal: The values do not follow a normal curve (Anderson–Darling, {p}): read Cp, Cpk and the expected % outside as rough. Look at the histogram: a long tail usually means waiting or rework in some cases; two humps mean two processes mixed.
normality.outliers: The {n} point(s) beyond the limits pull the tails. Without them the sample is {verdict} ({p}). Explain those points first, then judge the rest.
normality.few: Fewer than 8 measurements: no normality test is meaningful yet.

drift: Over the whole sample the values drift by {slope} {unit} per point (r = {r}). A slow drift is not a signal yet, but it will be.

proportion.real: The change from {p1} to {p2} is real ({p}): less than {chance} chance that it is noise. 95% interval for the difference: {low} to {high}.
proportion.noise: The change from {p1} to {p2} could be noise ({p}): with these numbers, a difference this size happens by chance about {chance} of the time. Measure more before you call it an improvement, or a problem.
proportion.borderline: The change from {p1} to {p2} is probably real ({p}), but not beyond doubt: about {chance} chance that it is noise. One more week of data would settle it.

means.real: The average moved from {m1} to {m2} ({diff}): real (Welch t = {t}, {p}). 95% interval for the change: {low} to {high}.
means.noise: The average moved from {m1} to {m2} ({diff}), but that could be noise ({p}): the two samples overlap too much to tell. Measure more or reduce the spread.
means.borderline: The average moved from {m1} to {m2} ({diff}): probably real ({p}), not yet beyond doubt. A few more measurements on each side would settle it.
means.need: Paste at least two values on each side.

size.alpha: Alpha is the risk of seeing a change that is not there: 5 % means one false alarm in twenty tests.
size.power: Power is the chance of seeing a change that is there: 80 % means you miss a real change one time in five.
size.proportionResult: Measure {n} units before and {n} after to tell {p0} from {p1}.
size.meanResult: Measure {n} values before and {n} after to see a change of {delta} {unit} when single values spread by {sd}.
size.need: Enter two different rates, alpha and power.

tips: Twenty values of the old process are the only proof your change worked. Start the chart today.
Limits come from the process, specs from the customer.
Control limits say what the process does; LSL and USL say what is needed. A stable process can still be a bad one.
A value inside the limits is noise, however bad it looks. A Nelson rule is a reason to walk to the floor.
p is not proof, but it stops arguments.
p = 0.002 means a difference this size happens by chance 2 times in 1,000. Decide with the number, then act.
A truck that waited two hours is real. Find its story; only then decide whether it belongs in the sample.

kinds.ask: A measurement, one at a time
kinds.help: One value per line, or a date or label and a value. Loading minutes, the weight of each pallet, the temperature at each check.

kinds.chart: Xbar-R (up to 8 per group) or Xbar-S (more than 8)
kinds.help: One group per line: a date or label, then the values of that group. Five pallets timed every day, three cartons weighed every hour. Up to 8 values per group give an Xbar-R chart, more an Xbar-S chart.

kinds.ask: Defective items out of the same number every time
kinds.help: A date or label, the defective items, then how many were checked: the same number every time, such as 50 sampled orders a day.

kinds.ask: Defective items out of a number that changes
kinds.chart: p chart, in the Sigma & Control Chart
kinds.help: A date, the defective items, then how many were handled that day. The p chart lives in the Sigma & Control Chart; this page hands your rows over.

kinds.ask: Defects counted on the same unit every time
kinds.help: A date or label and the number of defects found on one unit of the same size every time: label errors per shift, damages per full trailer.

kinds.ask: Defects counted on units that change in size
kinds.help: A date or label, the defects found, then the number of units checked: pallets audited, rooms inspected, 100 m² cleaned.

Early	34	10
Night	22	38
placeholders.attr:

chart.stable: No signal in {n} points: the ups and downs are the normal noise of this process. Reacting to single points will not help; to get a better number, change the process itself.
chart.signals: {count} signal(s) that are not normal noise. Look at those points first: what was different in volume, people, equipment or method? Then take the cause through 5 Whys.
chart.spread: The {chart} chart has {count} point(s) outside its limits: the spread inside those groups jumped. Look at what was mixed in them (two docks, two shifts, a new person).
chart.short: Fewer than 20 points: the limits are rough. Keep collecting before you trust a signal.
chart.phaseLevel: From {label} on, the centre line moved from {before} to {after} ({change}): {verdict}.
chart.phaseSpread: The spread (σ within) went from {before} to {after} ({change}).
chart.phaseCounts: For counts the spread follows the level, so the limits moved with it.

phaseVerdicts.borderline: probably real ({p}), not yet beyond doubt

chart.npVarying: The number checked is not the same on every row ({min} to {max}). An np chart needs the same number; the limits here follow each row, but the p chart is the right one for this data.
chart.sizes: The groups are not all the same size ({min} to {max}); each group gets its own limits.
chart.skipped: {n} row(s) left out, they lack what this chart needs: {need}
chart.needRows: Paste at least two rows with what this chart needs: {need}.

need.np: the defective items and the number checked, not more defective than checked
need.p: the defective items and the number handled
need.u: the defects and a number of units above 0

chart.pNote: Defective items out of a number that changes go on the p chart, with limits for each day's volume. The Sigma & Control Chart draws it, with the Nelson rules and the sigma level; open it with your rows.
chart.pNoDates: Only rows with a date can be handed over, and these have none. Put a date at the start of each row.

chi.real: The mix is not the same in every row ({p}): a pattern this strong comes from chance less often than {chance}. The biggest gap: {row} × {col}, {obs} counted where {exp} were expected if rows and columns had nothing to do with each other.
chi.borderline: The mix probably differs between the rows ({p}), but not beyond doubt. The biggest gap: {row} × {col}, {obs} counted where {exp} were expected. More data would settle it.
chi.noise: No real difference between the rows ({p}): the mix of these {total} counts is what chance alone would give. Do not chase a pattern in this table.
chi.low: {n} of {cells} cells expect fewer than 5 counts (the smallest {min}): the p-value is not reliable. Merge small rows or columns, or collect more data before you decide.
chi.need: Paste a table with a header row and at least two rows and two columns of counts (whole numbers, 0 or more).
chi.problem: {row} has more {col} than the other rows ({obs} against {exp} expected)
chi.action: Find out why {row} has more {col} than the others ({obs} against {exp} expected)

reg.sentence: Each extra {xUnit} changes {yName} by about {signed} (95% interval {low} to {high}).
reg.r2: r² = {r2}: {xName} explains {r2pct} of the ups and downs in {yName}; the other {rest} come from other causes.
reg.real: The link is real ({p}): a slope like this comes from chance less often than {chance}.
reg.borderline: The link is probably real ({p}), but not beyond doubt; a few more points would settle it.
reg.noise: The link could be noise ({p}): with these points a slope this size comes from chance {chance} of the time. Do not plan with it yet.
reg.miss: A typical point misses the line by about {sd}.
reg.cause: A link is not yet a cause: check on the floor that more {xMid} really changes {yName}, and that nothing else moves with both.
reg.need: Paste at least three pairs of numbers, x and y on each line.
reg.flat: All x values are the same: a line needs x values that differ.

excellent.label: Excellent
excellent.text: Kappa {kappa}: the judgement can be trusted. Keep the reference samples at the station and repeat the study once a year.

good.label: Good
good.text: Kappa {kappa}: acceptable for most uses. Go through the parts that were judged differently with the appraisers and sharpen the standard there.

poor.label: Needs work
poor.text: Kappa {kappa}: the judgement is not consistent enough to count defects with. Agree on a clear standard with photos and limit samples, train the appraisers, then run the study again.

attr.mixed: {n} part(s) judged differently from one trial to the next
attr.noStandard: Without a Standard column the study shows only whether the appraisers agree, not whether they are right.
attr.skipped: {n} row(s) with an empty cell were left out.
attr.need: Paste a table with a header row: Part, then Standard (optional), then one column per appraiser and trial, such as Anna 1, Anna 2, Ben 1, Ben 2. At least two parts.
attr.problem: The visual check is not consistent (kappa {kappa})
attr.action: Sharpen the standard for the visual check and train it (kappa {kappa})

good.label: Good
good.text: Total Gage R&R is {pct} of the study variation: the measurement system is good. Differences between parts are real differences.

depends.label: Depends on the use
depends.text: Total Gage R&R is {pct} of the study variation: acceptable depending on what the measurement decides, the cost of the gauge and the cost of a wrong call. Improve it if it sorts good from bad near a limit.

bad.label: Not acceptable
bad.text: Total Gage R&R is {pct} of the study variation: the measurement cannot tell the parts apart well enough. Fix the measurement before you base decisions on its data.

gage.repeat: Repeatability ({pct}) is the larger share: the gauge scatters when the same person measures the same part again. Look at the device, the fixture, the measuring point and the method.
gage.reprod: Reproducibility ({pct}) is the larger share: the operators measure differently. Agree on one method (where, how, how hard), write it down and train it.
gage.ndc: {ndc} distinct categories: the system can sort the parts into {ndc} groups; AIAG asks for 5 or more.
gage.ndcLow: Only {ndc} distinct categories: the system cannot sort the parts into enough groups; AIAG asks for 5 or more.
gage.interaction: The part × operator interaction is significant ({p}): some operators measure some parts differently. It counts as reproducibility.
gage.pooled: No part × operator interaction ({p}); it is pooled into repeatability, as AIAG and Minitab do.
gage.tolerance: Against the tolerance of {tol}, the R&R takes {pct}.
gage.need: Paste a table with a header row: Part, then one column per operator and trial, such as Anna 1, Anna 2, Anna 3, Ben 1 … Or three columns: part, operator, value. At least two parts.
gage.unbalanced: Every part needs the same number of trials by every operator, at least two. Check the table for missing values.
gage.problem: The measurement of {name} is not good enough (Gage R&R {pct} of the study variation)
gage.action: Improve the measurement of {name}: Gage R&R {pct} of the study variation

np.name: Late orders in 50 sampled a day
